San Antonio basketball has always been homonymous with winning. Since the NBA and ABA’s merger in 1976, San Antonio has only missed the playoffs five times. That’s only five out of 45 NBA seasons. From George Gervin to Artis Gilmore to David Robinson, the franchise always had a household star that helped lead the team to the postseason. They often got there, but they never experienced further success, making it to the Conference Finals a couple of times but never reaching the championship round.

That all changed with the arrival of Gregg Popovich to the Spurs’ bench. Popovich first got to San Antonio in 1987 as an assistant under then head coach Larry Brown. Pop had some coaching experience from his time with the United States Air Force. He was an assistant in San Antonio until 1992, when former owner Red McCombs fired the entire staff. He was brought back shortly after in 1994, after Pete Holt purchased the team, but this time Popovich was appointed as the team’s general manager.

The Spurs had a horrible 3 – 15 start to the 1996-97 regular season, as the team really struggled due to the absence of David Robinson, who was out with a back injury suffered in the pre-season, and the team looked miserable. In what was back then considered an arrogant move, Popovich fired Bob Hill as the head coach and appointed himself as his replacement. But looking back, that is probably the best decision in Spurs franchise history.

Robinson was out for most of the year, as he was only able to play in six games upon his return before breaking his foot, but the shorthanded Spurs did show some improvement under Popovich, finishing the season 17 – 47. Their disappointing 20 – 62 record landed them the first overall pick in the 1997 NBA Draft, which the team used to select Tim Duncan out of Wake Forest University. That’s when the Spurs dynasty began.

results.title: David Robinson Scores 71 Points to Win Scoring Title (1994)
results.description:
Entering the evening of April 20, 1994—four days prior to the conclusion of the regular season—San Antonio Spurs Center David Robinson held a slim scoring lead over Shaquille O'Neal, averaging 29.26 points per game to O'Neal's 29.03. That evening however, O'Neal made his move, scoring a then-career-high 53 points in a blowout win over the Minnesota Timberwolves. The performance thrust O'Neal into the scoring lead, pumping his average up to 29.32. 

With both Robinson and O'Neal holding steady in their team's penultimate games of the regular season (Robinson scored 29, O'Neal 27), that set up a final day showdown for the right to claim a scoring title that'd bounced back and forth between the two future Hall of Famers all year. 

Robinson's afternoon finale against the Los Angeles Clippers began innocently enough, accounting for 24 of his team's 37 first half points (18 of San Antonio's 20 in the first quarter, just 6 points in the second). With 43 points heading into the fourth, it seemed Robinson was in line to match or eclipse Shaq's 53-point outing just four days prior. And sure enough, Robinson delivered, scoring 17 points through the first 10 minutes of the fourth, notching 60 points for the first time in his career. 

But that's where things really got interesting. 

Following a Robinson jumper with two minutes remaining (62), the Spurs committed two fouls in subsequent possessions, one of which led to Robinson converting 1 of 2 free throws on the other end (63) & the other which culminated in Clippers guard Randy Woods being called for a technical foul, with a free throw converted by Robinson (64). Robinson's 64 points set a new franchise record, breaking the previous record of 63 points set by George Gervin, who was sitting courtside as a Spurs assistant coach for Robinson's performance. 

Robinson's final act came in rapid succession. First, he connected on his only 3-pointer of the day (67). A moment later, the Clippers failed to get back on defense following a made basket, leading to a Robinson breakaway dunk (69). Then, following a Bob Martin dunk, the Spurs worked the ball back over to Robinson, who rose above a double team to connect on his final shot of the day (71). 

"I looked up at the scoreboard,” Robinson later  told reporters. “I said, `71 points. Oh, my goodness!' It was unbelievable. My team has been behind me the whole year. They always push me to do a lot of individual things. As a leader, I just try to win games, but tonight they really wanted me to shoot it. When the game started they were looking for me almost every time down the court.”

With his performance, Robinson became just the fourth player in NBA history at the time to reach the 70-point plateau and the first to do so since David Thompson's 73-point performance in 1978 (coincidentally, Thompson's performance came in an end-of-season bid to usurp George Gervin for the scoring title. 

Robinson's outburst pushed his scoring average up to 29.78, sliding comfortably past O'Neal to retake the scoring lead. 

With Orlando's season finale coming later that same day, O'Neal had an opportunity to offer a retort. Alas, while he did finish with 32 points, it fell well short of the 68 he'd have needed to retake the scoring lead once and for all. 

All told, Robinson finished with 71 points on a 26-of-41 shooting from the field (.634 percent), 18-of-25 from the line (.720 percent), 14 rebounds, 5 assists, and 2 blocks.

Only the greatest ever did this. From Wilt’s unbreakable 100 to Luka’s shocking 73, these are the most unstoppable scoring nights in NBA history. When a player enters this elite group, it’s more than just a hot hand — it’s a legacy moment. 💯

🔥 Iconic Scoring Performances:

🏀 Wilt Chamberlain – 100 points (March 2, 1962)
The most iconic scoring performance in NBA history. Chamberlain's 100-point game for the Philadelphia Warriors against the New York Knicks remains unmatched. He set multiple records that night, including most points in a half (59) and most free throws made (28).  ​

🏀 Kobe Bryant – 81 points (January 22, 2006)
Bryant's 81-point game against the Toronto Raptors is the second-highest in NBA history. He scored 55 points in the second half, leading the Lakers to a comeback victory. This performance solidified Kobe's status as one of the game's greatest scorers.​

🏀 David Thompson – 73 points (April 9, 1978)
In a bid to win the scoring title, Thompson scored 73 points for the Denver Nuggets against the Detroit Pistons. Despite his efforts, he narrowly lost the title to George Gervin, who scored 63 points the same day.​

🏀 Luka Dončić – 73 points (January 26, 2024)
Dončić delivered a historic performance for the Dallas Mavericks against the Atlanta Hawks, scoring 73 points with remarkable efficiency. He became the youngest player to reach this mark, showcasing his exceptional talent. ​

🏀 David Robinson – 71 points (April 24, 1994)
Robinson scored 71 points for the San Antonio Spurs against the Los Angeles Clippers, securing the scoring title on the final day of the season. His dominant performance included 26 made field goals and 18 free throws.​

🏀 Donovan Mitchell – 71 points (January 2, 2023)
Mitchell's 71-point game for the Cleveland Cavaliers against the Chicago Bulls was a modern masterpiece. He added 11 assists and 8 rebounds, contributing to an overtime victory.​

Lillard scored 71 points for the Portland Trail Blazers against the Houston Rockets, making 13 three-pointers. His performance was one of the most efficient high-scoring games in NBA history.​

🏀 Elgin Baylor – 71 points (November 15, 1960)
Baylor's 71-point game for the Los Angeles Lakers against the New York Knicks was a record at the time. He also grabbed 25 rebounds, showcasing his all-around dominance.​

🏀 Michael Jordan – 69 points (March 28, 1990)
Jordan's career-high came in an overtime win against the Cleveland Cavaliers. He added 18 rebounds, 6 assists, and 4 steals in a complete performance.​

🏀 Devin Booker – 70 points (March 24, 2017)
At just 20 years old, Booker scored 70 points for the Phoenix Suns against the Boston Celtics, becoming the youngest player to reach this milestone.​

🏀 Klay Thompson – 60 points (December 5, 2016)
Thompson scored 60 points for the Golden State Warriors against the Indiana Pacers in just 29 minutes, showcasing his incredible shooting ability.

Derrick Gervin (born March 28, 1963) is an American former professional basketball player born in Detroit. He played in the National Basketball Association (NBA) and was the 1995 Israeli Basketball Premier League MVP, and a two-time top scorer in the Israel Basketball League, in 1996 and 1998. 

A 6' 8" forward from University of Texas at San Antonio (UTSA), Gervin was selected by the Philadelphia 76ers in the 4th round (20th pick, 90th overall) of the 1985 NBA draft. He played two seasons (1989–1991) in the National Basketball Association (NBA) as a member of the New Jersey Nets. He averaged 8.8 points per game in 77 games.

He was the 1995 Israeli Basketball Premier League MVP, playing and averaging 27.0 points per game for Hapoel Gvat/Yagur.[1] He was also a two-time top scorer in the Israel Basketball League, in 1996 and 1998.

Gervin's jersey was retired by UTSA in 2006. His older brother, George Gervin, played in the ABA from 1972 to 1976 and in the NBA from 1976 to 1986.
